title: Screen Time May Matter Most at Ages 1 and 6
summary:
When you look at a screen may matter as much as how long you look at it. Scientists from Inserm and the National University of Singapore followed 502 children in Singapore from ages 1 to 8. They found that extra screen time at ages 1 and 6 was linked to weaker school results at age 9 and weaker working memory at age 10 and a half. Working memory is the brain's way of holding and using information, like following instructions.

The link was strongest at age 1. The scientists said a baby's brain may be very sensitive at that age, because screens can replace talking and playing with grown-ups. Screen time at ages 2 and 3 showed no clear link, but the link came back at age 6, when children start school.

The study shows only a link, not proof that screens cause weaker results. Still, the scientists say less screen time is better. The World Health Organization and the American Academy of Pediatrics say no screens before 18 to 24 months, and less than one hour a day at ages 2 to 5.
why_it_matters: Knowing when screen time matters most can help you and your family choose more talking, playing, and other activities at the ages when your brain is learning fastest.

background_read: Scientists study how children grow and learn by watching the same children over many years and comparing what happens to them.
Working memory is the part of thinking that holds information in mind while you use it, like remembering instructions while you follow them.
Babies and young children learn a lot from talking and playing with grown-ups, so scientists want to know what happens when screens take the place of that time.
